Trump and Xi Keep Meeting. That’s Not a Good Sign.

More diplomacy may be a symptom of a deteriorating U.S.-China relationship

Alan Tang

Published on this site October 8, 2026

President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping have been seeing a lot of each other lately. Xi’s state visit to Washington, D.C. from September 23 to 25 followed Trump’s trip to Beijing in May, and the two leaders are already expected to meet again before the end of the year. They are scheduled to meet again at the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November and the G20 summit in Miami in December. If those meetings occur as planned, Trump and Xi will have met face-to-face four times in eight months.

By the usual standards of interstate diplomacy, this should be encouraging news and bring a sigh of relief to the entire world. Frequent meetings between the American and Chinese heads of state would seem to suggest that relations between the two often-adversarial nations have begun thawing.

Unfortunately, the opposite may be true. Xi arrived in Washington to extraordinary fanfare. He received military honors, a B-2 and F-22 flyover, a state dinner, a tour of Marine One and a visit to the National Archives. President Trump toasted a future of “harmony, peace, and success.” The White House even served Schramsberg “Blanc de Noirs,” the same brand of American sparkling wine used for Richard Nixon’s famous “Toast to Peace” with Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai in 1972.

The results were more modest.

The United States and China agreed to recommend lower tariffs on $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction. China committed to purchasing at least 10 million metric tons of American coal in both 2027 and 2028. Both governments established an investment mechanism, expanded trade discussions and created a channel for dialogue over artificial intelligence. China had also arrested 21 Chinese nationals in August after receiving information from U.S. law enforcement concerning fentanyl precursor trafficking. These were very real accomplishments. Very limited, real accomplishments.

If anything, the summit made clear that beyond the pomp and decor, the U.S. and China had very little worth compromising. The tariff agreement covered $60 billion in two-way trade and deliberately excluded sensitive products. Soybeans, America's largest agricultural export to China, were excluded from China’s tariff cuts. More importantly, the broader trade truce was extended for only two months, until January 10. Even after a presidential state visit, Washington and Beijing essentially bought themselves another 60 days to keep negotiating.

On one of Washington’s major priorities, critical minerals, there was no breakthrough. Critical minerals, including rare-earth metals, are essential inputs in everyday technology, from iPhones and Teslas to sensitive military hardware like F-35s, submarines, and Tomahawk missiles. The issue for American grand strategy is that China currently dominates the processing for many of them. The White House could only report that the countries would “continue to work” on American concerns over rare-earth and critical-mineral shortages. According to the Financial Times, China had fulfilled only about two-thirds of the rare-earth export commitments associated with the earlier Busan agreement.

The obvious conclusion is that the summit failed to live up to its hype. But that misses what may be the more important story. Washington and Beijing may be meeting so frequently not because they have more to agree on, but because they increasingly have less and less.

That would make the current moment almost the inverse of the rapprochement that began more than half a century ago.

When Richard Nixon landed in Beijing in February 1972, the United States and Communist China were hardly friends. They had not maintained normal diplomatic relations since the Communist victory in 1949, and they remained sharply divided over Taiwan and the international order amid the Cold War. Yet beneath those disagreements was an emerging strategic convergence. Both Washington and Beijing increasingly viewed the Soviet Union as a threat. China’s relationship with Moscow had deteriorated throughout the 1960s, culminating in armed border clashes between Chinese and Soviet forces in 1969. By the time Nixon arrived in Beijing, both countries had a compelling reason to disregard decades of prior hostility: each saw the other as a potential counterweight to Soviet power.

More importantly, the diplomacy between both nations actually produced tangible movement. The 1972 Shanghai Communiqué committed the two governments to continued high-level contact and further normalization. The U.S. and China agreed to facilitate scientific, cultural, educational, journalistic and commercial exchanges and to reduce barriers to bilateral commerce. Seven years later, they established formal diplomatic relations. Of course, the Communiqué did not create that strategic convergence alone, although it did help reveal and accelerate it.

The United States is spending billions of dollars trying to reduce its dependence on Chinese critical-mineral supply chains. In just the 18 months ending in June, The Wall Street Journal reported that Washington committed approximately $7.6 billion in non-equity support across more than 180 critical-mineral projects, while the Pentagon is aiming to eliminate Chinese-sourced metals from defense supply chains by 2030. Experts nevertheless estimate that fully unwinding Chinese dominance on rare-earths could take at least another decade.

In the meantime, Washington continues restricting Chinese access to strategically important American technologies, while Beijing has demonstrated its willingness to restrict exports of materials American manufacturers need.

This mutual de-risking reaches beyond the technicalities of economics. Washington and Beijing remain divided over Taiwan and military competition in the Indo-Pacific. Even the September summit failed to produce agreement on all of the proposed military-communication arrangements, according to reporting after the meeting.

There is consequently less room for the kind of strategic bargain that characterized earlier periods of engagement. Neither government appears prepared to concede on the issues it considers fundamental to their nation’s survival. Yet neither wants to absorb the enormous economic and security consequences of allowing the relationship to continue deteriorating.

So naturally, Trump and Xi meet.

Seen this way, the modest accomplishments of their summits begin to make more sense. A two-month trade truce delays the looming dynamic of economic competition. An AI channel may not reconcile competing American and Chinese visions for artificial intelligence, but it can provide a vague mechanism for managing the risks created by their competition. And on critical minerals, continued negotiations offer temporary relief from a crippling vulnerability the United States will need years to overcome. On every contentious issue, the summit could only treat its symptoms, not its underlying cause.

Then the clock winds back to midnight. The September summit illustrates the cycle almost perfectly. Trump and Xi arrived with major disputes unresolved. They extended their economic truce until January. They left the issue of rare earths unsettled. And before the year is over, they are scheduled to meet twice more. Over time, their summits become less and less indicative of rapprochement. In its crudest form, both nations are practicing a strategic form of procrastination.

That description should not be mistaken for an argument against diplomacy. The more adversarial the U.S.-China relationship becomes, the more valuable communication between Washington and Beijing may be. In September, the two governments agreed to establish a dedicated channel for AI-related risks and crises and committed to further military crisis communication. Those mechanisms could become particularly valuable precisely because the trust between the two nations is disappearing fast.

But preventing a relationship from spiraling into chaos is not the same thing as improving one.

That distinction matters because presidential diplomacy creates powerful imagery. A state visit, military ceremony and declarations of cooperation can make two countries appear to be moving toward one another even as their economic and security policies are moving apart drastically.

Nixon's 1972 visit offers the clearest contrast. Washington and Beijing then used summit diplomacy to begin dismantling barriers between them. Today's governments are spending billions constructing new ones.

The paradox is that this may make summit diplomacy even more necessary. When two governments possess substantial common interests, much of their relationship can operate below the presidential level. When disagreements become harder to contain, however, leaders may need to intervene repeatedly simply to prevent individual disputes from spilling into the broader relationship.

Trump-Xi diplomacy’s frequency should therefore not automatically be read as evidence of improving U.S.-China relations. It may instead be evidence of a structurally poisoned and weakening relationship, one that now requires constant intervention simply to keep its underlying disputes from escalating into military confrontation in Taiwan, the South China Sea, and beyond.

Nearly fifty-five years ago, Nixon’s trip to Beijing demonstrated that two hostile nations had discovered reasons to move closer together. In 2026, Trump and Xi may be demonstrating the reverse. For now, another summit can buy another truce, perhaps another round of negotiations or another few months of stability. But postponement is not resolution, and extravagant ceremonies cannot indefinitely conceal the decline of the relationship.

One day, there may be nothing left for another summit to postpone.
